new_statements.quote: Comme élément supra-segmental, il y a par exemple le ton. Etant donné que le bànkón est une langue à tons, une étude des tons qui jouent un rôle distinctif dans cette langue sera envisagée, et suivant aussi les deux axes paradigmatique et syntagmatique.
new_statements.translation: As a supra-segmental element there is, for example, tone. Given that Bankon is a tone language, a study of the tones that play a distinctive role in this language will be undertaken, following the paradigmatic and syntagmatic axes as well.
new_statements.citation: Atindogbé, Gratien Q. 1990. Esquisse phonologique du Bankon (dialecte lombe). Mémoire de maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé. 111 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 13 (PDF p. 18), Introduction, 'La Théorie'; tone inventory §1.1.1 pp. 14-16
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (116 PDF pages; MPG PuRe copy of the Yaounde maitrise). Locator check: PDF p. 18 = printed p. 13 (page number '13' at foot of the page image, section 'La Theorie' of the introduction). Rendered the page image (page render, 110 dpi) and read it: the passage is there, paragraph 3: "Comme element supra-segmental, il y a par exemple le ton. Etant donne que le ɓàŋkón est une langue à tons, une etude des tons qui jouent un role distinctif dans cette langue sera envisagee, et suivant aussi les deux axes paradigmatique et syntagmatique." The only difference from the reported quote is the spelling of the language name: the page writes it with implosive b-hook and eng (ɓàŋkón), the repor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bankon is described as a tone language with five tonemes (low, mid, high, rising, falling); the source says nothing about word stress or a culminative accent. The only 'accent' remark (p. 75) concerns English loanwords whose H-B tone melody is attributed to English initial stress, which implies stress is not a native Bankon category in this author's analysis but is not stated as such.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. p. 75: the H-B tonal sequence on disyllables is rare in native words (about 6/1400) and found mainly in English loans (bótà 'butter', sóndʒà 'soldier', drósì 'dress', kótì 'coatee', kótìn 'cotton'), explained by the stressed first syllable of the English source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexemes and noun/verb stems, citation forms); no phrase-level stress discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Atindogbé 1990 describes the Bankon dialect proper (spoken north of the Wouri estuary, Dibombari, Moungo), which ALCAM treats as one of two dialects (bankon, lombe) of a language it calls 'lombe' — hence the thesis subtitle '(dialecte lombe)'. Glottolog bank1256 = Bankon/Abo [abb]; the sister lect Lombe/Barombi is baro1252 [bbi]. Hyman & Lionnet 2011 call the same language Abo (A42).

new_statements.translation: §21: 'The dynamic [= stress] accent always rests on the stem syllable and is therefore not marked. [Morphology. The noun classes. §22 Class 1 ...] Footnote 1) The tone marks, however, are far from always written, and the above rule is not always observed ...' §20: 'On tone. The pronoun as genitive particle mostly has high tone, e.g. mút nú sòngo "the man of the hunt, the hunter". Likewise the demonstrative pronoun and the subject pronoun of the verb as a rule have high tone, e.g. á bòn ...'

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Atindogbé 1990, Lombe dialect): tone language, no stress statement. Spellenberg 1922 agrees that Bankon has tone (§19-20, tone marks, Hochton rules) and ADDS a stress statement: the dynamic accent always falls on the stem (root) syllable and is unmarked. Compatible with the tonal record (no competing placement held by the project); the languoid reading becomes 'tonal, with predictable stem-syllable (root-initial) stress per the 1922 primary description'. Caveat: read from search snippets of three scans, not from a page image; a browser download of Google Books UAcmAAAAMAAJ (full view) or HathiTrust mdp.39015050687709 / uva.x001506363 p. 25 would upgrade this to a page-verifi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spellenberg treats Bankon (Bo/Abo, A42) as having lexical/grammatical tone written with tone marks (§19 Tonzeichen, §20 Zur Tonlehre: high tone on genitive, demonstrative and subject pronouns, etc.) and, separately, a dynamic (expiratory stress) accent that 'always rests on the stem syllable' (i.e. the root-initial syllable after the class/agreement prefix) and is therefore left unmarked in his transcription. Stress is thus predictable from morphology (stem syllable), non-contrastive, in a tone language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the visible text (§21 appears to consist of this one sentence: the snippet passes directly from it to 'Formenlehre').
new_statements.exceptions: none: 'immer' (always) on the stem syllable; the footnote on the same page qualifies the tone-mark practice (marks not always set, rule not always observed), not the stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Spellenberg 1922 describes Bo/Bankon (Abo), Bantu A42, Cameroon (Basel Mission field, Littoral); the catalog source Atindogbé 1990 describes the Lombe dialect of Bankon.

sources.note: Whole thesis is a structuralist phonology (tones, vowels, consonants, syllable/word structure). States p. 13 that Bankon is a tone language ('le bànkón est une langue à tons') and inventories five tonemes (bas, moyen, haut, montant, descendant, pp. 14-16). Contains no statement on word stress/accent in Bankon; the only mention of 'accent' (p. 75) is that the rare H-B tonal sequence occurs mostly in English loanwords (bótà 'butter', sóndʒà 'soldier') and is attributed to English initial stress. Verified against page images (PDF pp. 18 and 80).
